title: Pulsed control of an entanglement-breaking index: thermal valleys, a certified valve, and its open-close asymmetry
abstract: The entanglement-breaking index of a channel is the number of self-compositions after which all entanglement with a reference system is destroyed. In a thermal qubit collision loop whose round is affine in the bath polarisation p, some circuits have thermal valleys: on an interior window of p the index falls below its infinite-temperature value. Rounds at different p compose exactly, so every schedule of polarisations defines a composite channel whose entanglement-breaking status can be certified in ball arithmetic. A gated search of 33 million random circuits finds no valley with contrast above about 3e-3, with an interior maximum near index 90, and yields six certified targets. At the reference target, held inside its window for 88 rounds, a centred excursion to p = 0.05 restores entanglement at exactly eight rounds: every shorter centred pulse certifiably fails, and so do the same eight rounds at the start. A 53-round pulse certifiably beats the static protocol, a depth-three valley is walked down its staircase by pulse duration, and a 1.2 per cent coherent tilt of the ancilla opens the switch at fixed population. Closing the switch costs 21 to 35 rounds. The asymmetry is not one of local rates, which agree to within about two per cent at matched circuit positions (certified). It is one of distance and response: closing must remove an entanglement margin 2.2 times larger, and while hot rounds added to a window hold act almost independently, window rounds added to a hot hold act collectively. Near the crossing, the lever of the log-margin is that of a linear approach to the entanglement-breaking boundary, with no free parameter. At the reference target, depolarising noise of about $4ν/n$ per round kills a signature of size $ν$ read after $n$ rounds: 1.3e-4 for the static signal, 6.5e-6 for the eight-round switch.
summary: This theoretical work analyzes the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel controlled by varying bath polarizations. The authors identify a 'thermal valley' structure exhibiting a pronounced open-close asymmetry in how the entanglement switch can be manipulated. By using certified arithmetic, they provide rigorous bounds on these quantum resource diagnostics.
main_problem: The paper investigates the entanglement-breaking index of a quantum channel, specifically analyzing how this index behaves when the channel is composed of rounds with varying bath polarizations.
main_result: A specific 'valve' structure was identified where entanglement can be restored by a precise, short pulse (8 rounds), demonstrating a significant open-close asymmetry compared to the cost of closing the valve (21-35 rounds).
method: The analysis relies on rigorous mathematical certification using ball arithmetic (Arb) to determine the sign of the minimum eigenvalue of the partially transposed Choi matrix, diagnosing entanglement status.
model_or_system: The system models a message qubit interacting with two ancillas in a three-qubit feedback circuit, where the interaction is controlled by a tunable bath polarization parameter, $p$.
key_observables: Entanglement-breaking index ($n_{EB}$), contrast of thermal valleys, and the minimum eigenvalue ($\lambda_{\min}$) of the partially transposed Choi matrix.
important_parameters: Bath polarization $p$ (ranging from 0 to 1), number of rounds ($n$), and the required pulse length for switching states.
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes the channel action is affine in $p$, and the results are certified using high-precision arithmetic, though experimental realization requires extremely low error rates.
figures_summary: The notes reference tables detailing certified valley targets and a 'Pulse Atlas' quantifying the minimal pulse lengths required to switch the composite state between certified PPT (closed) and NPT (open) states.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the entanglement-breaking index, searching for 'thermal valleys' in the index as a function of bath polarization, and culminating in a detailed analysis of the observed asymmetry between opening and closing the entanglement switch.
why_interesting: The study provides a highly quantitative, certified framework for diagnosing subtle quantum resource properties (entanglement) in open quantum systems, which is crucial for designing robust quantum protocols.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

Mode OPEN (blue): hold 0.4016, pulses to p = 0.05 (solid) and 0.24 (dashed); mode CLOSE (orange): hold 0.05, pulses to 0.4016 (solid) and 0.62 (dashed). Above zero the composite is PPT (entanglement broken), below zero NPT (entangled). Dots mark the minimal switching pulse; the values at k = 0 and the switch at k = 8 (solid blue) are certified.
